study.title: Psalm 36 - the human corruption and the incomparable goodness of God
study.overview: This psalm contrasts two realities. In verses 1 to 4, sin appears as an inner force that corrupts the wicked, eliminating the fear of God and producing evil words, plans, and ways. In verses 5 to 9, the psalmist raises his eyes to the greatness of God: his goodness, faithfulness, justice, and care sustain all creation and, in a special way, those who take refuge in him. In verses 10 to 12, he asks that this goodness continue upon those who know the Lord, supplicates protection against the arrogance of the wicked and concludes with confidence that the practitioners of wickedness will fall and will not rise.

outline.title: Evil that is born of the heart without fear of God
outline.explanation: The text describes the wicked as one dominated by pride, deception, and rejection of wisdom. Sin is not only presented as an external act, but as an inner disposition that plans evil and does not depart from it.

outline.title: The goodness of God that sustains creation and gives life
outline.explanation: In contrast to human disorder, the psalmist celebrates the mercy, faithfulness and righteousness of the Lord, whose care reaches heaven, clouds, mountains and depths, preserving men and animals and offering shelter, food, water and light to those who trust in him.

outline.title: Prayer for protection and certainty of the final judgment on the wicked
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks that the goodness and justice of God reach the faithful, prays not to be shaken by the violence of the arrogant and concludes that those who practice wickedness will fall definitively.

study.context: The notes indicate that the psalm was composed of David, the servant of the LORD, but the exact moment is uncertain. Matthew Henry suggests that it may have been written when David suffered opposition from Saul or Absalom; Adam Clarke records these hypotheses and also mentions another proposal, that of a captivity scenario, without treating it as sure. The content itself shows a devotional contrast: the wickedness of the enemies on the one hand, and the confidence in the goodness of God on the other.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that sin is deeply deforming: when there is no fear of God, the human being proceeds to justify his own wickedness, speak with deceit and persevere in evil. At the same time, the text presents God as absolutely reliable and superior to all creation in goodness, faithfulness and justice. His mercy is neither weak nor indifferent; it sustains life, provides shelter, and preserves those who seek it. Theologically, there is a strong contrast between the moral ruin of the wicked and the life received from God. The psalmist also trusts that divine justice will not fail: evil will not have the final word, and the wicked will fall. This reading is consistent with the evangelical perspective that God is holy, graceful and just, without identifying this psalm with a specific denominational system.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm contrasts the wickedness with the world of wisdom created and sustained by the Lord; the fools despise what is wise and good in persecuting evil.
David is presented as a servant of the LORD, and this condition is highlighted as honor; the psalm leads the reader to consider the sin and goodness of God afterwards.
The psalmist trusts that the disorder caused by the wicked will end when they find their ruin.

questions: In which areas can I be treating sin with tolerance, instead of odding it as destructive?
How does God's goodness appear as a shelter, sustenance and light in my concrete routine?
Is my trust more in the strength of the arrogant or in the righteousness of the Lord that finally overthrows evil?
study.practice: This week, read the psalm slowly and highlight the words linked to the character of God: goodness, faithfulness, justice, life and light. Then identify a practical attitude of refuge in the Lord: abandon a morally doubtful practice, ask for direction in prayer before acting, or demonstrate patient confidence when suffering opposition. At the same time, ask God to give you a heart that does not normalize evil, but recognize and reject it.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not clearly inform the historical occasion of the composition. The notes offer hypotheses, but do not allow us to state with certainty whether the psalm was written because of Saul, Absalom or captivity. There is also a small textual difficulty in verse 1, highlighted by Adam Clarke, about the exact form of the phrase; therefore, the interpretation should be done with caution and supported in the general flow of the psalm.
